question: Which city served as the capital of the Pallava dynasty?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Kanchipuram.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Kanchipuram (Kanchi), on the Palar river in northern Tamil Nadu, was the capital of the Pallavas from the age of Simhavishnu to the end of the dynasty (कांचीपुरम — पल्लवों की राजधानी)

 

• Kanchi was a great centre of Sanskrit learning with a ghatika (Brahmanical college), and later became one of the seven sacred cities of Hinduism.

 

• The Chinese pilgrim Hiuen Tsang visited Kanchipuram in the 7th century and described it as a centre of Buddhism, Jainism and Hinduism.

 

• Pallava power was based on the fertile northern Tamil plains (Tondaimandalam), which contrasts with the Pandya heartland far to the south.

 

• The Pallava kings built their finest temples in and around Kanchi and at the port of Mamallapuram, about 60 km away.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Kanchipuram is famous even today for its silk sarees and its many temples, including the Kailasanatha and Vaikuntha Perumal temples.

 

• The Pallavas fought a long series of wars with the Chalukyas of Badami, whose capital was Vatapi.

 

• The Muttaraiyar chiefs of the Cauvery delta acknowledged the Pallava kings of Kanchipuram as their overlords.

 

• Mamallapuram (Mahabalipuram), the main Pallava seaport, lies on the Coromandel coast and handled trade with Southeast Asia, which spread Pallava art to Java, Cambodia and elsewhere.

 

NOTE

 

• Madurai (Option 1): Madurai was the capital of the Pandya kings, whose kingdom lay in the far south of Tamil Nadu around the Vaigai river. The Pandyas were often rivals of the Pallavas but their seat of power was never Kanchi.

 

• Thanjavur (Option 2): Thanjavur became prominent as the Chola capital after Vijayalaya and reached its glory under Rajaraja I, who built the Brihadeeswara temple there. It belongs to the medieval Chola age, not to the Pallava dynasty.

 

• Uraiyur (Option 4): Uraiyur (near Tiruchirappalli) was the early Chola capital in the Sangam age. It was a trading and textile town of the ancient Cholas, and so cannot be the Pallava seat.

question: Who is regarded as the founder of the Pallava dynasty, who ruled from about 575 to 600 AD?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Simhavishnu.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Simhavishnu (c. 575-600 AD) is regarded as the real founder of the imperial line of the Pallavas, who made Kanchipuram their capital and defeated the Kalabhras and neighbouring Tamil rulers (सिंहविष्णु — पल्लव वंश का संस्थापक)

 

• He is credited with breaking the power of the Kalabhras, who had ruled the Tamil country for a long period, and extended Pallava control up to the Kaveri.

 

• His son and successor Mahendravarman I inherited a strong kingdom and then had to face the growing Chalukya threat from the north-west.

 

• The Pallava line he began lasted for about three centuries, until it was overshadowed by the revived Cholas under Aditya I.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Pallavas first appear in the Deccan as officers of the Satavahanas, and early Pallava charters were written in Prakrit and then Sanskrit.

 

• Pallava rulers were mostly devotees of Shiva or Vishnu, yet they patronised Buddhism and Jainism too in the early years.

 

• The Pallava kingdom was known as Tondaimandalam, with Kanchi as its political centre.

 

• Pallava inscriptions use Sanskrit and Tamil; the Pallava Grantha script later influenced the scripts of Southeast Asia, such as those of Cambodia and Java.

 

NOTE

 

• Mahendravarman I (Option 2): Mahendravarman I was the son of Simhavishnu and ruled from about 600 to 630 AD. He was a gifted playwright and builder but he is remembered as the second great king, not the founder.

 

• Narasimhavarman I (Option 3): Narasimhavarman I (Mamalla) was the grandson of Simhavishnu and became famous for defeating the Chalukya Pulakesin II and capturing Vatapi. He belongs to the third generation of the line.

 

• Nandivarman II (Option 4): Nandivarman II (Pallavamalla) ruled in the 8th century, when the dynasty was already well established, and he built the Vaikuntha Perumal temple. He came long after the founding of the dynasty.

question: The Sanskrit farce 'Mattavilasa Prahasanam' was written by which Pallava ruler?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Mahendravarman I.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Mahendravarman I (600-630 AD) wrote the Sanskrit satirical play Mattavilasa Prahasanam ('the farce of drunken sport'), which pokes fun at Kapalika ascetics and Buddhist monks (मत्तविलास प्रहसन — महेन्द्रवर्मन प्रथम)

 

• He bore the titles Vichitrachitta, Gunabhara and Mattavilasa, which show his love of art, music and drama.

 

• He first followed Jainism but was later converted to Shaivism by the Nayanar saint Appar.

 

• He introduced rock-cut cave temples in the Tamil country, which are called Mandagapattu-type cave shrines.

 

• His reign saw the Chalukya king Pulakesin II invade Pallava lands and seize the northern portion of the kingdom.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Mahendravarman I is credited with the Sanskrit work Bhagavadajjukiyam as well, and with the treatise Dakshinachitra on painting.

 

• The Mandagapattu inscription calls his temple a shrine built without brick, timber, metal or mortar.

 

• A Pallava ruler's farce was acted at the Kanchi court, which shows the royal patronage of Sanskrit drama.

 

• Mahendravarman I also ordered the Mamandur and Mandagapattu cave shrines, and his title Chettakari points to his role as a builder of temples.

 

NOTE

 

• Narasimhavarman I (Option 1): Narasimhavarman I was the son of Mahendravarman I and is known as a warrior and builder, who took the title Vatapikonda after destroying Vatapi. He is not recorded as the author of any Sanskrit farce.

 

• Narasimhavarman II (Option 3): Narasimhavarman II (Rajasimha) is famous as the builder of the Shore Temple and the Kailasanatha temple at Kanchi. His fame rests on temple architecture and not on a satirical drama.

 

• Paramesvaravarman I (Option 4): Paramesvaravarman I was the Pallava ruler who fought the Chalukya Vikramaditya I and lost ground in the war. His reign is known for battles and for the Kuram plates, and not for the Mattavilasa Prahasanam.

question: Which Pallava ruler took the title 'Vatapikonda' after capturing the Chalukya capital Vatapi?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Narasimhavarman I.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Narasimhavarman I (630-668 AD) defeated the Chalukya king Pulakesin II and captured and destroyed Vatapi, for which he took the title Vatapikonda ('conqueror of Vatapi') (वातापिकोंडा — नरसिंहवर्मन प्रथम)

 

• His campaign was an act of revenge for the defeat his father Mahendravarman I had suffered when Pulakesin II had seized the northern Pallava territory.

 

• He won the decisive battle at Manimangalam near Kanchi and then marched into the Chalukya country.

 

• He also adopted the title Mamalla ('great wrestler'), from which the port town of Mamallapuram takes its name.

 

• The Chinese traveller Hiuen Tsang came to Kanchipuram during his reign.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Pallava navy under Narasimhavarman I is said to have helped a Sri Lankan prince, Manavarma, regain his throne.

 

• The victory over the Chalukyas was recorded by later Pallava charters,.

 

• Narasimhavarman I was a devotee of Shiva, and the Pallava rathas at Mamallapuram were carved during his reign.

 

• A rock inscription of Narasimhavarman I recording his victory is still to be seen at Badami, which is the Chalukya capital he conquered.

 

NOTE

 

• Mahendravarman I (Option 1): Mahendravarman I was the father of the conqueror and actually lost the northern part of his kingdom to Pulakesin II. He could not take Vatapi, so the title is not his.

 

• Simhavishnu (Option 2): Simhavishnu was the founder of the line and ruled before the Chalukya-Pallava wars reached their peak. His campaigns were against the Kalabhras and Tamil neighbours and not against Vatapi.

 

• Narasimhavarman II (Option 4): Narasimhavarman II (Rajasimha) ruled in the late 7th and early 8th centuries, a period of peace and temple building. He was a builder of temples and did not conquer Vatapi, which had been taken decades earlier.

question:
Consider the following statements about Narasimhavarman I:

1. He defeated the Chalukya king Pulakesin II.

2. He founded the port-town of Mamallapuram (Mahabalipuram).

3. He built the Kailasanatha temple at Kanchipuram.

Which of the above statements is/are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Only 1 and 2.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The correct choice is 1 and 2: Narasimhavarman I defeated Pulakesin II and founded Mamallapuram (Mahabalipuram) and had the five monolithic rathas cut there; statement 3 is wrong because the Kailasanatha temple was begun by Rajasimha (नरसिंहवर्मन प्रथम — ममल्लपुरम, पाँच रथ)

 

• The Kailasanatha temple at Kanchi was built by Narasimhavarman II (Rajasimha) and completed by his son Mahendravarman III.

 

• The five rathas (Dharmaraja, Bhima, Arjuna, Draupadi, Nakula-Sahadeva) are monolithic structures carved from single rocks in the time of Narasimhavarman I.

 

• His title Mamalla gave the town its name, Mamallapuram.

 

• The Kanchi temple therefore belongs to a later reign than the king described in the stem.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Mamallapuram monuments, including the Shore Temple and the rathas, are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

 

• The Arjuna's Penance (Descent of the Ganga) relief at Mamallapuram is a famous open-air rock sculpture of the Pallava age.

 

• Rock-cut Pallava monuments are grouped into the Mahendra and Mamalla styles after the two kings.

 

• Mamallapuram's carved monuments include the Arjuna's Penance relief, the Krishna Mandapa and the five rathas, and all of these belong to the Mamalla phase of Pallava art.

 

NOTE

 

• Only 2 and 3 (Option 2): This combination takes statement 3 as true. The Kailasanatha temple at Kanchipuram was the work of Rajasimha and his son Mahendravarman III, so statement 3 fails, and the combination also drops the true statement 1.

 

• Only 1 and 3 (Option 3): Dropping statement 2 and keeping 3 cannot work. Mamallapuram was founded and named after Narasimhavarman I, and statement 3 is an error since the Kanchi temple was built later.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 4): Marking every statement as true overlooks the fact that the Kailasanatha temple was raised by Narasimhavarman II. Only the first two statements describe Narasimhavarman I correctly.

question: The Shore Temple at Mamallapuram was built during the reign of:
solution_text:
The correct answer is Narasimhavarman II (Rajasimha).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Shore Temple at Mamallapuram, on the Bay of Bengal, was built by Narasimhavarman II (Rajasimha) and is a structural temple built of cut stone blocks (शोर टेम्पल, ममल्लपुरम — राजसिंह)

 

• It marks the shift in Pallava architecture from rock-cut caves and monolithic rathas to free-standing structural temples.

 

• Rajasimha also began the Kailasanatha temple at Kanchi, which was completed by his son Mahendravarman III.

 

• The temple is a fine specimen of the Dravidian style with its pyramid-like tower (vimana) rising in stages.

 

• Along with the nearby rathas and rock reliefs, it forms part of the monuments of Mamallapuram, a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Shore Temple complex contains shrines to both Shiva and Vishnu.

 

• The Pallava ruler Rajasimha used titles such as Atyantakama and Ranajaya.

 

• The Dharmaraja Ratha, the tallest of the five rathas, is regarded as a model for later Dravidian vimanas.

 

• The Shore Temple has two main shrines facing east and west, and a third small shrine between them, so the complex is not a single sanctum.

 

NOTE

 

• Narasimhavarman I (Option 1): Narasimhavarman I is associated with the five monolithic rathas and the rock-cut mandapas at Mamallapuram. His works are carved out of living rock and are not built of stone blocks like the Shore Temple.

 

• Mahendravarman I (Option 2): Mahendravarman I introduced rock-cut cave temples such as those at Mandagapattu and Mahendravadi. He did not build structural temples, so he cannot be credited with the Shore Temple.

 

• Nandivarman II (Option 3): Nandivarman II (Pallavamalla) belongs to the 8th century and built the Vaikuntha Perumal temple at Kanchi. The Shore Temple is the earlier work of Rajasimha.

question: The Virupaksha temple at Pattadakal was modelled on which Pallava temple?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Kailasanatha temple, Kanchipuram.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Virupaksha temple at Pattadakal was modelled on the Kailasanatha temple at Kanchipuram, built by the Pallava king Rajasimha (विरुपाक्ष मंदिर, पट्टदकल — कांची के कैलासनाथ मंदिर की नकल)

 

• Chalukya king Vikramaditya II is said to have been so impressed by the Kanchi temple, after defeating the Pallavas, that his queen Lokamahadevi built a similar temple.

 

• It shows how the long wars between the Pallavas and the Chalukyas also led to a flow of artistic ideas.

 

• Pattadakal is in Karnataka and the temples combine Nagara (northern) and Dravidian (southern) features.

 

• It was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and its ten temples show the early development of Chalukya architecture.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Pattadakal was the coronation site of the Chalukya kings of Badami.

 

• The Kailasanatha temple at Kanchi was built on the Vegavathy river bank and has a fine sculptural programme.

 

• The Virupaksha temple is also called Lokeshvara temple in inscriptions.

 

• Pattadakal lies close to Badami and Aihole in Bagalkot district, so these three Chalukya sites can be seen together as a single circuit.

 

NOTE

 

• Shore Temple, Mamallapuram (Option 2): The Shore Temple stands at the seaside in Mamallapuram, quite far from Kanchi, and is a smaller structural temple of Rajasimha. It was not the pattern for Pattadakal's Virupaksha temple.

 

• Brihadeeswara temple, Thanjavur (Option 3): The Brihadeeswara temple at Thanjavur was built by the Chola ruler Rajaraja I in the early 11th century. This is long after the Chalukya temple of Pattadakal, so it cannot have been the model.

 

• Dharmaraja Ratha, Mamallapuram (Option 4): The Dharmaraja Ratha is one of the five monolithic rathas carved in the time of Narasimhavarman I. It is a rock-cut monolith and not a structural temple, and it is not the temple copied at Pattadakal.

question: Which Chinese pilgrim visited the Pallava capital Kanchipuram in the 7th century AD?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Hiuen Tsang.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Hiuen Tsang (Xuanzang) visited Kanchipuram during the reign of the Pallava king Narasimhavarman I, in the 7th century (ह्वेनसांग — कांचीपुरम की यात्रा)

 

• He also visited the court of the Chalukya king Pulakesin II and wrote about the great battle on the Narmada between Pulakesin II and Harsha.

 

• His account describes Kanchi as a large city with Buddhist monasteries and Jain and Hindu temples, which shows its religious variety.

 

• He travelled during the reign of Harshavardhana and returned to China with hundreds of Buddhist manuscripts.

 

• His book is called Si-Yu-Ki (Records of the Western World).

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Hiuen Tsang studied at Nalanda under the teacher Shilabhadra.

 

• He was in India from about 629 to 645 AD, and was present at Harsha's religious assembly at Kannauj and Prayag.

 

• Kanchi had been a place of learning since the early Pallava age.

 

• Hiuen Tsang also visited Nalanda, Kannauj, Kamarupa and other places, and returned to China in 645 AD with a large collection of Buddhist texts and relics.

 

NOTE

 

• Fa-Hien (Option 1): Fa-Hien came to India much earlier, during the reign of Chandragupta II (Gupta period) in the early 5th century. He did not travel in the Pallava age and did not reach Kanchi.

 

• I-Tsing (Option 2): I-Tsing came in the later 7th century and stayed mainly at Nalanda and in Sumatra, writing on monastic rules. He is not credited with a visit to the Pallava capital in Narasimhavarman's time.

 

• Sung-Yun (Option 4): Sung-Yun was a Chinese monk who visited north-western India in the 6th century, around the Gandhara region. He lived and travelled long before the Pallava rulers described here.

question: The Dravidian style of temple architecture began under which of the following dynasties?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Pallavas.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Pallavas introduced the cutting of temples out of rock in the south, and the Dravidian style of temple architecture begins with their rule (द्रविड़ शैली का आरंभ — पल्लव शासन)

 

• Pallava architecture developed in four stages: Mahendra style (cave temples), Mamalla style (monolithic rathas), Rajasimha style (structural temples) and Nandivarman style.

 

• The pyramid-shaped vimana and the pillared mandapa are basic features of this style, and they were perfected later by the Cholas.

 

• The structural temples at Kanchipuram and the Shore Temple show the final stage of the dynasty's architectural skill.

 

• Later dynasties, including the Cholas at Thanjavur, took the Pallava model forward on a larger scale.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Dravidian style is marked by vimana, gopuram, mandapa and a water tank; the Nagara style has a curvilinear shikhara.

 

• Vesara, a mixed style, was developed in the Deccan under the Chalukyas.

 

• The Pallava kings Mahendravarman I and Narasimhavarman I are linked to rock-cut work, while Rajasimha is linked to structural work.

 

• Dravidian temples have features such as the vimana over the sanctum, a pillared mandapa, enclosure walls and, in later centuries, tall gateway towers called gopurams.

 

NOTE

 

• Chalukyas of Badami (Option 1): The Chalukyas of Badami built cave temples at Badami and structural temples at Aihole and Pattadakal in a blend of styles. Their characteristic contribution is the Vesara style and not the origin of the Dravidian style.

 

• Rashtrakutas (Option 3): The Rashtrakutas created the Kailasa temple at Ellora and the Elephanta shrines, and they followed the already existing Pallava and Chalukya models. They arrived after the Dravidian style had already begun.

 

• Eastern Chalukyas (Option 4): The Eastern Chalukyas ruled from Vengi in Andhra and are noted more for their political history and patronage of Telugu literature than for founding any architectural style.

question:
Assertion (A): Narasimhavarman I assumed the title 'Vatapikonda'.

Reason (R): He defeated the Chalukya king Pulakesin II and captured and destroyed his capital Vatapi.
option_1: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
option_2: A is true but R is false
option_3: A is false but R is true
option_4: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
solution_text:
The correct answer is Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Both statements are true and R explains A: the title Vatapikonda means 'conqueror of Vatapi' and it was taken because Narasimhavarman I defeated Pulakesin II and destroyed the Chalukya capital (वातापिकोंडा — वातापी विजेता)

 

• The Pallava king undertook the campaign to avenge his father Mahendravarman I, whose northern territories had been seized by Pulakesin II.

 

• The Chalukya king was beaten at Manimangalam and the Pallava army then advanced to Vatapi (Badami) in Karnataka.

 

• Titles in ancient India often recorded a particular victory, as with Pulakesin II's title Dakshinapatheshvara after the Narmada battle.

 

• The Pallava conquest of Vatapi ended Chalukya power for some years, until Vikramaditya I revived it.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Vatapi is the modern Badami in Bagalkot district of Karnataka.

 

• The conquest of Vatapi in the 640s is the most celebrated event in Pallava history.

 

• Chalukya recovery came under Vikramaditya I, who defeated Paramesvaravarman I.

 

• Mahendravarman I's rock-cut caves are called Mahendra style, while Narasimhavarman I's monolithic work is Mamalla style, and the later structural phase is Rajasimha style.

 

NOTE

 

• Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A (Option 1): This choice says that R is true but fails to explain A, which is wrong here. The reason is exactly why the title was taken, so the explanation is direct and complete.

 

• A is true but R is false (Option 2): This choice accepts A as true but treats R as false. In fact the capture and destruction of Vatapi after the defeat of Pulakesin II are well recorded, so R cannot be rejected.

 

• A is false but R is true (Option 3): This choice makes A false, but the title Vatapikonda is well known as belonging to Narasimhavarman I, the victor over Pulakesin II.

question:
Match the following:

a. Mahendravarman I

b. Narasimhavarman I

c. Narasimhavarman II (Rajasimha)

d. Ravikirti

i. Composer of the Aihole Inscription

ii. Builder of the Shore Temple

iii. Took the title Vatapikonda

iv. Author of Mattavilasa Prahasanam
solution_text:
The correct answer is a-iv, b-iii, c-ii, d-i.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The correct matching is a-iv, b-iii, c-ii, d-i: Mahendravarman I wrote the farce Mattavilasa Prahasanam, Narasimhavarman I was Vatapikonda, Rajasimha built the Shore Temple, and Ravikirti composed the Aihole Inscription (मिलान — महेन्द्रवर्मन, नरसिंहवर्मन, राजसिंह, रविकीर्ति)

 

• Mahendravarman I was a ruler of literary tastes who also bore titles like Vichitrachitta and introduced rock-cut cave temples.

 

• Narasimhavarman I won at Manimangalam and destroyed Vatapi, the Chalukya capital, to avenge his father.

 

• Narasimhavarman II is linked with structural temples at Mamallapuram and Kanchi, and his reign was peaceful.

 

• Ravikirti was the Jain court poet of Pulakesin II who wrote the Sanskrit eulogy at Aihole.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Mattavilasa Prahasanam makes fun of Kapalikas and Buddhist monks and is a Sanskrit farce of one act.

 

• The Aihole Inscription is dated in the Saka year 556, which corresponds to 634-35 AD.

 

• Rajasimha's Kailasanatha temple at Kanchi was completed by his son Mahendravarman III.

 

• The Mattavilasa Prahasanam is a one-act Sanskrit farce, and it is the work of a Pallava king who had a great liking for drama and music.

 

NOTE

 

• a-iii, b-iv, c-ii, d-i (Option 1): This arrangement gives the farce to Narasimhavarman I and the title Vatapikonda to Mahendravarman I. The conqueror of Vatapi was the son, while the playwright was the father, so the first two links are swapped.

 

• a-iv, b-ii, c-iii, d-i (Option 3): Here the title Vatapikonda stays with Narasimhavarman II and the Shore Temple is given to Narasimhavarman I. Rajasimha built the Shore Temple, and the conqueror of Vatapi was Narasimhavarman I, so these pairs are wrongly crossed.

 

• a-i, b-iii, c-ii, d-iv (Option 4): In this arrangement the Aihole Inscription is credited to Mahendravarman I and the play to Ravikirti. Ravikirti was a Chalukya court poet, and the play was by the Pallava king, so the first and last pairs are exchanged.

question:
Consider the following statements about the Pallava ruler Mahendravarman I:

1. He wrote the Sanskrit play Mattavilasa Prahasanam.

2. He took the title Vatapikonda.

3. Pulakesin II seized the northern part of his kingdom.

Which of the above statements is/are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Only 1 and 3.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Here 1 and 3 hold true: Mahendravarman I wrote Mattavilasa Prahasanam and lost the northern part of his kingdom to Pulakesin II; statement 2 is wrong since Vatapikonda was the title of his son Narasimhavarman I (महेन्द्रवर्मन प्रथम — पुलकेशिन से हार)

 

• Pulakesin II's invasion of the Pallava lands took place in the reign of Mahendravarman I, who is believed to have been defeated at Pullalur, though he was able to hold Kanchi.

 

• The title of conqueror of Vatapi was won only when Narasimhavarman I avenged his father by capturing the Chalukya capital.

 

• Mahendravarman I's reign (600-630 AD) thus saw both literary achievement and military setback.

 

• He started the rock-cut tradition of Pallava temple building.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• His cave temples are found at Mandagapattu, Mahendravadi, Mamandur, Dalavanur and Tiruchirappalli.

 

• Narasimhavarman I carried the Pallava arms to Vatapi after the setback his father had suffered.

 

• Tradition says he was a Jain who turned to Shaivism through the saint Appar.

 

• Mahendravarman I's reign saw Jains and Shaivas compete for royal favour, and his shift to Shaivism is seen in the Shiva shrines he built as cave temples.

 

NOTE

 

• Only 1 (Option 1): Taking only statement 1 leaves out the invasion by Pulakesin II. The Chalukya king did seize the northern part of the Pallava kingdom in his reign, so statement 3 is also true.

 

• Only 1 and 2 (Option 2): Statement 2 is false, because the title Vatapikonda belongs to Narasimhavarman I. Any combination that includes it is wrong, and this one also drops the true statement 3.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 3): Accepting all three means believing the father was the conqueror of Vatapi. In fact he lost territory to Pulakesin II, and the conquest of Vatapi was made by his son.

question: The Chalukyas of Badami originally had their first capital at Aihole, but later shifted it to:
solution_text:
The correct answer is Vatapi.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Chalukya capital was first at Aihole and later shifted to Vatapi (modern Badami) in Karnataka, from which the dynasty is called the Chalukyas of Badami (वातापी/बादामी — चालुक्यों की राजधानी)

 

• The founder Pulakesin I established the dynasty at Vatapi and made it the seat of Chalukya power.

 

• Vatapi was destroyed by the Pallava king Narasimhavarman I, but it was recovered under Vikramaditya I and remained important until the end of the dynasty.

 

• Badami is famed for its rock-cut cave temples carved in the red sandstone hills, which include Hindu, Jain and Buddhist caves.

 

• The monuments of Aihole, Badami and Pattadakal form the three major sites of early Chalukya art.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Aihole is called the cradle of Indian temple architecture because it has experiments in many temple styles.

 

• Badami's cave temples include one for Vishnu dated to 578 AD in the time of Mangalesha.

 

• The Badami Chalukya dynasty ruled from the 6th to the middle of the 8th century.

 

• The rock-cut caves at Badami were dug in four main caves, with Cave 1 for Shiva, Caves 2 and 3 for Vishnu and Cave 4 for the Jain tirthankaras.

 

NOTE

 

• Kalyani (Option 1): Kalyani (modern Basavakalyan) was the capital of the Western Chalukyas, who rose in the late 10th century. It was not the early capital of the Badami line.

 

• Vengi (Option 2): Vengi in coastal Andhra Pradesh was the seat of the Eastern Chalukyas, who set up a separate kingdom after Pulakesin II died. It was never the capital of the main Badami line.

 

• Manyakheta (Option 4): Manyakheta (Malkhed) was built by the Rashtrakuta king Amoghavarsha I as his capital. It was founded by the dynasty which replaced the Badami Chalukyas and not by them.

question:
Consider the following statements:

1. Pulakesin I founded the Chalukya dynasty with Vatapi as its capital.

2. Pulakesin II took the title Dakshinapatheshvara.

3. Pulakesin II was the last ruler of the Chalukyas of Badami.

Which of the above statements is/are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Only 1 and 2.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Only 1 and 2 stand correct here: Pulakesin I founded the dynasty at Vatapi, and Pulakesin II bore the title Dakshinapatheshvara ('lord of the southern region'); statement 3 is false as the last ruler was Kirtivarman II (पुलकेशिन प्रथम, द्वितीय — दक्षिणापथेश्वर)

 

• Pulakesin II was the greatest Chalukya king, who defeated Harsha on the Narmada and extended his power from the Narmada to the Kaveri.

 

• He was himself defeated and killed by the Pallava Narasimhavarman I, but the dynasty went on after him through Vikramaditya I and others.

 

• The final ruler, Kirtivarman II, was defeated by Dantidurga, who founded the Rashtrakuta dynasty.

 

• The dynasty therefore ended roughly a century after Pulakesin II's death.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Pulakesin II's titles included Prithvi Vallabha and Parameshvara, besides Dakshinapatheshvara.

 

• His court poet Ravikirti composed the Aihole Prashasti.

 

• After his death, his brother's line in Vengi became the Eastern Chalukyas.

 

• Pulakesin I performed the Ashvamedha sacrifice to proclaim his sovereignty, and he made the hill fort of Vatapi the seat of the new kingdom.

 

NOTE

 

• Only 1 (Option 2): Statement 1 alone would ignore the title Dakshinapatheshvara, which is correctly credited to Pulakesin II. So statement 2 is also correct and this choice is incomplete.

 

• Only 3 (Option 3): Statement 3 stands alone here, but it is false. The Chalukya dynasty went on for about a century after Pulakesin II, and its last ruler was Kirtivarman II.

 

• Only 2 and 3 (Option 4): This pair accepts statement 3 together with 2, but statement 3 is wrong because Pulakesin II was not the last king. It also leaves out the correct statement 1.

question: Harshavardhana was defeated on the banks of the Narmada by which southern ruler?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Pulakesin II.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Pulakesin II of the Chalukyas of Badami defeated Harshavardhana on the banks of the Narmada (the Battle of the Narmada, about 618 AD), which checked Harsha's advance towards the Deccan (पुलकेशिन द्वितीय — हर्ष को नर्मदा तट पर हराया)

 

• The event is recorded in the Aihole Inscription, composed by Ravikirti, and also in the account of Hiuen Tsang.

 

• After this victory Pulakesin II took the title Dakshinapatheshvara, and the Narmada became the boundary between the two empires.

 

• This was one of the few reverses in Harsha's career and it kept the south free from his control.

 

• The Chalukya king himself later fell before the Pallava Narasimhavarman I.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Harsha belonged to the Pushyabhuti (Vardhana) dynasty and had his capital at Kannauj.

 

• Harsha's death in 647 AD was followed by political fragmentation of North India.

 

• Ravikirti's Aihole Prashasti compares Pulakesin II with great kings of the past.

 

• Pulakesin II's victory made the Narmada the boundary between Harsha's empire and the Chalukya kingdom, and his rule extended to the Kaveri in the south.

 

NOTE

 

• Narasimhavarman I (Option 1): Narasimhavarman I was a Pallava king and an opponent of Pulakesin II, not of Harsha. He defeated the Chalukya king at Manimangalam and had no part in the contest on the Narmada.

 

• Dantidurga (Option 2): Dantidurga was the founder of the Rashtrakuta dynasty in the 8th century, over a hundred years after Harsha died. He could not have fought Harsha, and he only overthrew the later Chalukya king Kirtivarman II.

 

• Govinda III (Option 3): Govinda III was a Rashtrakuta ruler of about 800 AD who defeated the Pala Dharmapala and the Pratihara Nagabhata II. He lived long after Harsha's time.

question: The Aihole Inscription, which praises the Chalukya king Pulakesin II, was composed by:
solution_text:
The correct answer is Ravikirti.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Aihole Inscription (Aihole Prashasti), in Sanskrit, was composed by the Jain poet Ravikirti, the court poet of Pulakesin II (रविकीर्ति — ऐहोल प्रशस्ति)

 

• It records Pulakesin II's victory over Harshavardhana on the Narmada and his campaigns against the Pallavas and others.

 

• The inscription is found on the Meguti Jain temple at Aihole in Karnataka, which Ravikirti himself had built.

 

• It is a prashasti, a eulogy in elegant Sanskrit verse, and is the main source for Pulakesin II's reign.

 

• The inscription gives its date both in the Saka era and in years counted from the Mahabharata war, which makes it a useful dating record.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Aihole Inscription is dated in the Saka year 556, which corresponds to 634-35 AD.

 

• Its author compared himself to Kalidasa and Bharavi in the final verses.

 

• Aihole is known as the 'City of Temples' because of its large number of old temples.

 

• Ravikirti's Meguti temple at Aihole is one of the earliest dated stone temples in India, and the inscription in it is the source of its date.

 

NOTE

 

• Harishena (Option 2): Harishena composed the Allahabad Pillar Inscription praising the Gupta emperor Samudragupta. It belongs to the 4th century and to a northern dynasty, not to Pulakesin II.

 

• Banabhatta (Option 3): Banabhatta was the court poet of Harshavardhana, who wrote the Harshacharita and the Kadambari. He served Pulakesin II's rival, so he could not have composed the Chalukya eulogy.

 

• Kalidasa (Option 4): Kalidasa is the famous Sanskrit dramatist of the Gupta age and the author of the Shakuntala and Meghaduta. He lived a couple of centuries before Pulakesin II and left no inscription for him.

question: Which Chalukya ruler took the title 'Dakshinapatheshvara' (lord of the southern region) after defeating Harsha?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Pulakesin II.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Pulakesin II assumed the title Dakshinapatheshvara after defeating Harsha on the Narmada and gaining control over the southern region (दक्षिणापथेश्वर — पुलकेशिन द्वितीय)

 

• His other titles in the notes include Prithvi Swami, and he is considered the greatest king of the Chalukyas of Badami.

 

• His reign (c. 608-642 AD) saw the expansion of Chalukya power over the Deccan and also the rise of conflict with the Pallavas.

 

• His court poet Ravikirti composed the Aihole Prashasti which records these titles and victories.

 

• The Persian king Khusrau II is said to have exchanged embassies with him.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The title Dakshinapatha was also used for the whole region south of the Narmada in ancient texts.

 

• Pulakesin II's brother Kubja Vishnuvardhana was made viceroy of Vengi, where the Eastern Chalukya line began.

 

• He was killed in the Pallava attack on Vatapi around 642 AD.

 

• Dakshinapatha meant the whole southern part of India south of the Narmada and the Vindhyas, and the title was also used by the Satavahanas in earlier times.

 

NOTE

 

• Vikramaditya I (Option 1): Vikramaditya I was the son of Pulakesin II, who recovered the Chalukya kingdom after the Pallava conquest. He regained Vatapi, but the title for the victory over Harsha belongs to his father.

 

• Kirtivarman II (Option 2): Kirtivarman II was the last Chalukya of Badami and was overthrown by Dantidurga. He lived about a century after Pulakesin II, so he could not have defeated Harsha.

 

• Tailapa II (Option 4): Tailapa II founded the Western Chalukya dynasty of Kalyani in the 10th century. He lived more than three centuries after Harsha, and is therefore unconnected with this title.

question:
Consider the following statements about the Aihole Inscription:

1. It is written in Sanskrit.

2. It was composed by the Chinese traveller Hiuen Tsang.

3. It was written in praise of the Chalukya king Pulakesin II.

Which of the above statements is/are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Only 1 and 3.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The valid statements are 1 and 3: the Aihole Inscription is a Sanskrit prashasti in praise of Pulakesin II; statement 2 is wrong because its author was the Jain poet Ravikirti and not Hiuen Tsang (ऐहोल अभिलेख — संस्कृत, रविकीर्ति)

 

• Hiuen Tsang was only a visitor to Pulakesin II's court, who wrote a separate account in Chinese describing the Narmada battle.

 

• The inscription records the defeat of Harsha and the early conflicts with the Pallavas, and is the best source on Pulakesin II.

 

• It is at Aihole in Karnataka, which means the 'City of Temples' and has the Lad Khan temple.

 

• A native court-poet and a foreign pilgrim thus give two independent sources for the same event.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Lad Khan temple at Aihole is among the oldest Hindu temples and was originally a hall with a pillared porch.

 

• Hiuen Tsang's account, Si-Yu-Ki, is in Chinese.

 

• The Aihole Prashasti dates a key year from the Mahabharata war and the Saka era.

 

• The Aihole Prashasti also tells of the Chalukya wars against the Kadambas, the Gangas, the Mauryas of the Konkan and the Latas before the Harsha campaign.

 

NOTE

 

• Only 1 and 2 (Option 1): This pair includes the Hiuen Tsang claim as correct. The inscription is a Sanskrit text composed by a local Jain poet, so statement 2 fails, and the pair also leaves out the correct statement 3.

 

• Only 2 and 3 (Option 3): Choosing statements 2 and 3 ignores that the inscription is in Sanskrit. Statement 2 is a mistake as well, since the Chinese pilgrim did not compose the inscription.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 4): Accepting all three statements overlooks the mistaken authorship in the middle one. The eulogy was composed by Ravikirti and it was not the work of Hiuen Tsang.

question: Who avenged the defeat of his father Pulakesin II by defeating the Pallava king Paramesvaravarman I?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Vikramaditya I.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Vikramaditya I, son of Pulakesin II, defeated the Pallava ruler Paramesvaravarman I and so avenged the defeat and death of his father at the hands of Narasimhavarman I (विक्रमादित्य प्रथम — पल्लवों से बदला)

 

• After Pulakesin II's death the kingdom had gone through some confusion, with Pallava control over Vatapi for a time.

 

• Vikramaditya I restored Chalukya power and recovered Vatapi, ending the Pallava occupation.

 

• His success shows the pattern of alternating victories in the long Chalukya-Pallava contest.

 

• Later, Vikramaditya II also defeated the Pallavas and entered Kanchi, an event linked with the Virupaksha temple.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Chalukya-Pallava conflict lasted for over a century, from Mahendravarman I to Nandivarman II.

 

• Paramesvaravarman I was the successor of Narasimhavarman I.

 

• Vikramaditya II entered Kanchi but spared the Kailasanatha temple and gave gifts to it.

 

• The Chalukya line went on through Vinayaditya and Vijayaditya to Vikramaditya II, who ruled in the first half of the 8th century.

 

NOTE

 

• Kirtivarman II (Option 2): Kirtivarman II was the last Chalukya of Badami, and he was overthrown by the Rashtrakuta Dantidurga. He did not avenge Pulakesin II, since he lost the kingdom itself.

 

• Vikramaditya II (Option 3): Vikramaditya II was a later king and a great-grandson of Vikramaditya I, remembered for entering Kanchi and for his queen Lokamahadevi's temple. The revenge for Pulakesin II came a couple of generations earlier.

 

• Pulakesin I (Option 4): Pulakesin I was the founder of the dynasty and the great-grandfather of Vikramaditya I, who lived before Pulakesin II. He could not have avenged a defeat that was suffered later.

question: Lokamahadevi, who built the Virupaksha temple at Pattadakal, was the queen of which Chalukya ruler?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Vikramaditya II.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Lokamahadevi was the chief queen of the Chalukya king Vikramaditya II, and she built the Virupaksha temple at Pattadakal in his reign (लोकमहादेवी — विक्रमादित्य द्वितीय की रानी)

 

• The temple was modelled on the Kailasanatha temple at Kanchipuram, which the king saw after his victory over the Pallavas.

 

• Her sister, another queen of the king, built the nearby Mallikarjuna temple, which shows royal women as patrons of architecture.

 

• Pattadakal is a UNESCO World Heritage Site in Karnataka with about ten temples that show the blending of Nagara and Dravidian styles.

 

• Vikramaditya II belonged to the Chalukyas of Badami and ruled in the first half of the 8th century.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Vikramaditya II is credited with the capture of Kanchi from the Pallava Nandivarman II.

 

• The Virupaksha temple has fine sculptures of scenes from the Ramayana and Mahabharata.

 

• The Virupaksha temple is still a living place of worship and is now a protected monument.

 

• Lokamahadevi's sister Trailokyamahadevi built the Mallikarjuna temple, and both temples at Pattadakal were set up to celebrate the king's victory over the Pallavas.

 

NOTE

 

• Vikramaditya I (Option 1): Vikramaditya I was the great-grandfather of Vikramaditya II, and is known for recovering Vatapi from the Pallavas. He ruled several decades before the Pattadakal temple was built.

 

• Pulakesin II (Option 2): Pulakesin II was the great warrior who defeated Harsha, ruling in the first half of the 7th century. Pattadakal's Virupaksha temple was built a century after his reign.

 

• Kirtivarman II (Option 4): Kirtivarman II was the last king of the dynasty and was removed by Dantidurga. He ruled after the temple had been built, and he is not linked with Lokamahadevi.

question:
Match the following branches/dynasties with their capitals:

a. Chalukyas of Badami

b. Eastern Chalukyas

c. Western Chalukyas

d. Pallavas

i. Vengi

ii. Kalyani

iii. Vatapi

iv. Kanchipuram
solution_text:
The correct answer is a-iii, b-i, c-ii, d-iv.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The correct matching is a-iii, b-i, c-ii, d-iv: Badami Chalukyas ruled from Vatapi, Eastern Chalukyas from Vengi, Western Chalukyas from Kalyani and the Pallavas from Kanchipuram (राजधानियाँ — वातापी, वेंगी, कल्याणी, कांची)

 

• The Chalukyas ruled from the 6th to the 12th century as three related but separate dynasties.

 

• The Badami branch was the earliest, with its greatest king Pulakesin II, and declined after his death in 642 AD.

 

• The Eastern branch grew out of a viceroyalty in the eastern Deccan, while the Western branch rose in the late 10th century.

 

• The Pallava capital was in the Tamil country and served as the rival centre during the Chalukya-Pallava wars.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Kalyani is today's Basavakalyan in Karnataka, and Vengi lay in present-day Andhra Pradesh.

 

• Eastern Chalukyas later continued as feudatories of the Cholas.

 

• The Badami and Pallava capitals were each captured by the other side at some stage.

 

• The Chalukyas of Badami are also called the Early Chalukyas, and the Western Chalukyas are sometimes called Later Chalukyas of Kalyani.

 

NOTE

 

• a-i, b-iii, c-ii, d-iv (Option 1): Here Vengi and Vatapi are exchanged. Vatapi was the Badami capital and Vengi was the seat of the Eastern branch, so the first two links are wrongly crossed.

 

• a-iii, b-ii, c-i, d-iv (Option 3): In this arrangement Kalyani and Vengi change places. Kalyani belonged to the Western Chalukyas, while Vengi was the Eastern Chalukya seat in coastal Andhra, so the middle pairs are wrong.

 

• a-iii, b-i, c-iv, d-ii (Option 4): This arrangement gives Kanchipuram to the Western Chalukyas and Kalyani to the Pallavas. Kanchi was in the Tamil country and Kalyani in the north Karnataka region, so the last two pairs are interchanged.

question: The Eastern Chalukya kingdom of Vengi arose out of the viceroyalty of a prince after the death of which king?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Pulakesin II.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• After the death of Pulakesin II in 642 AD, the viceroyalty of Vishnuvardhana (Kubja Vishnuvardhana) in the eastern Deccan became an independent kingdom, the Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi (पुलकेशिन द्वितीय के बाद — वेंगी के पूर्वी चालुक्य)

 

• Vishnuvardhana was the brother of Pulakesin II and had been appointed to govern the Andhra region after its conquest.

 

• The Pallava attack on Vatapi and the death of the king weakened the central authority, and made the separation easy.

 

• The branch ruled Vengi in present-day Andhra Pradesh until about 1130 CE.

 

• They then continued as feudatories of the Cholas until about 1189 CE.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Eastern Chalukya rulers were patrons of Telugu literature; Nannaya began translating the Mahabharata into Telugu in the court of Rajaraja Narendra.

 

• Rajaraja Chola's daughter Kundavai was married into the Eastern Chalukya family.

 

• The Eastern Chalukya line was linked with the Cholas by repeated marriage alliances.

 

• Kubja Vishnuvardhana ruled Vengi around 624 AD, and the dynasty he founded stayed in power in coastal Andhra for about five centuries.

 

NOTE

 

• Pulakesin I (Option 2): Pulakesin I was the founder of the dynasty at Vatapi, and ruled long before the Eastern branch came up. The separation occurred after Pulakesin II, the greatest king of the line, had died.

 

• Vikramaditya II (Option 3): Vikramaditya II ruled in the 8th century, about a hundred years after the Eastern Chalukya state had already been created. Its origin is placed in the 7th century.

 

• Kirtivarman II (Option 4): Kirtivarman II was the last Badami Chalukya, who lost his kingdom to Dantidurga around the middle of the 8th century. The Vengi kingdom had become independent long before him.

question: The Western Chalukyas of Kalyani were founded by:
solution_text:
The correct answer is Tailapa II.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Tailapa II founded the Western Chalukyas of Kalyani in the late 10th century, after he overthrew the weakened Rashtrakutas, whom he had served as a feudatory (तैलप द्वितीय — कल्याणी के पश्चिमी चालुक्य)

 

• The dynasty ruled from Kalyani, modern Basavakalyan in Karnataka, up to the end of the 12th century.

 

• They are called 'Western' simply to distinguish them from the Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi, who were a separate branch of the same period.

 

• They claimed descent from the Badami Chalukyas, and this claim linked the new dynasty with the older royal family.

 

• Their rise marked the end of Rashtrakuta power in the Deccan.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Western Chalukya kings fought a long series of wars with the Cholas over the Vengi region.

 

• Vikramaditya VI of this line is the hero of Bilhana's Vikramankadevacharita.

 

• Somesvara I moved the capital to Kalyani.

 

• The Kannada poet Ranna and the Sanskrit scholar Vijnaneshwara, who wrote the Mitakshara law commentary, belonged to the Western Chalukya cultural world.

 

NOTE

 

• Dantidurga (Option 1): Dantidurga founded the Rashtrakuta dynasty by overthrowing the Badami Chalukya Kirtivarman II. Tailapa II later destroyed the Rashtrakutas, who were the successors of Dantidurga, so Dantidurga cannot be the founder of Kalyani's line.

 

• Pulakesin II (Option 2): Pulakesin II was the great king of the Badami branch who defeated Harsha. He lived more than three centuries before the Western Chalukyas came into being.

 

• Vishnuvardhana (Option 4): Vishnuvardhana was the prince who founded the Eastern Chalukya line in Vengi. His dynasty was a different branch, and it did not rule from Kalyani.

question: Which Rashtrakuta chief overthrew his Chalukya overlord and founded the Rashtrakuta dynasty?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Dantidurga.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Dantidurga defeated the Chalukya king Kirtivarman II (Kirti Varman II) and founded the Rashtrakuta dynasty in the middle of the 8th century (दंतिदुर्ग — राष्ट्रकूट वंश का संस्थापक)

 

• He is believed to have been first a feudatory of the Chalukyas of Badami, before he turned against his overlord.

 

• The overthrow of Kirtivarman II, the last Badami Chalukya, ended that dynasty's rule in the Deccan.

 

• The Rashtrakutas were of Kannada origin, and Kannada was their mother tongue, and they were devoted worshippers of Shiva.

 

• The dynasty ruled in the Deccan until the 10th century, when it was destroyed by Tailapa II.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Dantidurga is also credited with the Hiranyagarbha ritual, which was meant to give a Kshatriya status to a non-Kshatriya king.

 

• Dantidurga's successor was his uncle Krishna I.

 

• The Samangad plates and other records describe the career of Dantidurga.

 

• After the fall of Kirtivarman II, the Rashtrakutas became the dominant power of the Deccan, and Dantidurga took titles such as Maharajadhiraja and Parameshvara.

 

NOTE

 

• Amoghavarsha (Option 1): Amoghavarsha I ruled for 64 years and is known for founding Manyakheta as the capital, along with his support for literature. He came three generations after Dantidurga and did not overthrow Kirtivarman II.

 

• Krishna I (Option 2): Krishna I was Dantidurga's uncle and succeeded him. He completed the overthrow of Chalukya power and built the Kailasa temple, but the dynasty had already been founded by his nephew.

 

• Govinda III (Option 3): Govinda III was a famous Rashtrakuta warrior who defeated Dharmapala and took part in the Kannauj struggle. He lived decades after the dynasty came into existence.

question:
Consider the following statements about the Chalukyas:

1. The Eastern Chalukyas ruled from Vengi in present-day Andhra Pradesh.

2. The Western Chalukyas were founded by Dantidurga.

3. The Eastern Chalukyas later carried on as feudatories of the Cholas.

Which of the above statements is/are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Only 1 and 3.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Statements 1 and 3 are the true ones: the Eastern Chalukyas ruled from Vengi in Andhra and later served the Cholas as feudatories; statement 2 is false because the Western Chalukyas were founded by Tailapa II (चालुक्य शाखाएँ — वेंगी और कल्याणी)

 

• Dantidurga founded the Rashtrakutas, whom the first Western Chalukya, Tailapa II, had once served as a feudatory.

 

• The names 'Eastern' and 'Western' simply distinguish the two later branches, which were separate dynasties of the same period.

 

• The Eastern branch lasted until about 1130 CE and then served the Cholas, while the Western branch ruled from Kalyani until the end of the 12th century.

 

• The three Chalukya branches thus shared a common origin in Badami but had different histories.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Eastern Chalukyas were descended from Kubja Vishnuvardhana, brother of Pulakesin II.

 

• Western Chalukya rule at Kalyani is noted for its Gadag-style temples in the Vesara tradition.

 

• Kalyani became a famed cultural centre under Vikramaditya VI.

 

• Chola-Chalukya wars were fought for Vengi, and it was a Chola-Chalukya prince who finally became the Chola king Kulottunga I in 1070 AD.

 

NOTE

 

• Only 1 (Option 2): Taking only statement 1 ignores the later fate of the Eastern Chalukyas, who did become feudatories of the Cholas. So statement 3 is true and this answer is incomplete.

 

• Only 1 and 2 (Option 3): Statement 2 goes wrong by giving the founding of the Western Chalukyas to Dantidurga, who in fact founded the Rashtrakutas. This pair also drops the correct statement 3.

 

• Only 2 and 3 (Option 4): Statement 2 again is the flaw in this pair, and this pair also leaves out the correct statement 1 about the Vengi kingdom.
